newsitem.title: SPAIN: BT/MCI telecoms deal historic, Telefonica says.
newsitem.headline: BT/MCI telecoms deal historic, Telefonica says.

text.p: Spain's Telefonica said on Friday its decision to form a strategic alliance with British Telecommunications and U.S. group MCI would convert it into a world leader in the telecoms industry.
"This is an historic accord. This is the most important accord that a Spanish company has signed in recent years," Telefonica chairman Juan Villalonga told Reuters in an interview.
"It's a necessary condition, but not sufficient, to continue along on the path that we have started to turn ourselves into one of the five world leaders in telecommunications."

Telefonica, which is the ninth largest telecoms firm in the world by revenues and the biggest provider in the Spanish-speaking world, said the much-awaited alliance would "reshape the global telecommunications landscape".
In the deal, announced early on Friday, the Spanish operator will acquire about one percent of BT in exchange for about two percent of Telefonica.
In addition, Telefonica's international subsidiary TISA will create a pan-American joint venture with MCI, which is in the process of merging with BT.
Shares in Telefonica -- privatisation of which was completed earlier this year -- were steady around 3,565 pesetas at 1200 GMT, having risen around four percent earlier this week ahead of the deal.
Villalonga, who looked exhausted and distracted, refused to be drawn on why the Spanish operator had opted for MCI instead of AT&T as a partner in Latin America.
He said only that Telefonica had made a thorough analysis of potential partnerships and had chosen the alliance that would best serve its interests.

"We believe the alliance we signed is the one that best defends the interests of our shareholders, our clients and our employees," Villalonga said. "This alliance will consolidate the share value of Telefonica, making it safer, more stable."

Telefonica is already allied with AT&T through a European venture called Unisource but it has been flirting with a number of others in the past eight months in search of a U.S. operator to consolidate its Latin American and U.S. operations.
News that Telefonica had chosen BT/MCI broke accidently on Monday when Portugal Telecom announced that both it and Telefonica had formed an alliance with BT/MCI.
Telefonica quickly denied that a deal had been reached and insisted it was still in talks with both AT&T and BT/MCI.
Villalonga then flew to Portugal and on Wednesday announced that Telefonica and Portugal Telecom had made a share swap deal to strengthen their Latin American interests.

On Friday, he insisted that Telefonica's stake in Unisource was completely compatible legally with the new BT/MCI partnership, which would concentrate principally in Latin America and less so in Europe, where Unisource operates.

But Villalonga, appointed chairman after the new conservative government came to power in May last year, said Telefonica had been in contact with its partners in Unisource to look at any possible implications of the BT/MCI accord on its Unisource partnership.
Industry sources said AT&T had been lobbying hard to keep Telefonica from switching allegiance.
